label: Body and fitness
rationale: What someone's body can do: see, run, play sport, keep going; often said about yourself in the negative (me warui, tairyoku nai).
mixUps: English adjectives (short-sighted, fast, athletic, fit) all become noun + ga + word: the eyes are bad, the legs are fast, the motor nerves are good, the stamina is there. Speed is hayai, coordination is ii, and stamina takes aru/nai, not ii.

targets.trap: Not warui me o motteru ('have bad eyes'): Japanese makes the eyes the subject, me ga warui. English 'short-sighted' has no everyday one-word match either: kinshi and shiryoku ga warui are the terms you hear at eye exams. 'My eyes got worse' is me ga waruku natta, not warui ni natta.
targets.use: Said about yourself to explain glasses or squinting: me warui kara... Casual speech drops ga. 'My eyes got worse' is me ga waruku natta.
targets.notes: The opposite, me ga ii, means good eyesight. 'Has a good eye' (for people or things) is miru me ga aru.

example.romaji: me warui kara, megane nai to nanimo mienai n da.
example.ja: 目悪いから、メガネないと何も見えないんだ。
example.english: My eyesight's bad, so I can't see a thing without my glasses.

examplePolite.romaji: me ga warui node, megane ga nai to nanimo mienai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 目が悪いので、メガネがないと何も見えないんです。
examplePolite.english: My eyesight is poor, so I can't see anything without glasses.

targets.verbSense: hayai: fast; the same word also means early
partners: shigoto (shigoto ga hayai: a fast worker)
henji (henji ga hayai: quick to reply)
targets.use: Said about kids, classmates and athletes: ano ko, ashi hayai ne, often with ga dropped. Japanese puts the speed in the legs, ashi ga hayai; hashiru no ga hayai also works. The opposite is ashi ga osoi (a slow runner).
targets.notes: ashi ga hayai also means food spoils fast (namamono wa ashi ga hayai).

example.romaji: ano ko, kurasu de ichiban ashi hayai n da.
example.ja: あの子、クラスで一番足速いんだ。
example.english: That kid's the fastest runner in the class.

examplePolite.romaji: ano ko wa kurasu de ichiban ashi ga hayai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: あの子はクラスで一番足が速いんです。
examplePolite.english: That child is the fastest runner in the class.

targets.kana: うんどうしんけいがいい
targets.trap: Not asurechikku (in Japanese that's an obstacle-course playground): say undou shinkei ga ii. supootsu ga tokui and undou ga dekiru (good at sports) are also natural.
targets.use: The everyday 'athletic, coordinated': ano hito, undou shinkei ii yo ne, with ga dropped. The opposite, undou shinkei ga nai, is common self-deprecation, and so is undou onchi (uncoordinated).

example.romaji: undou shinkei ii ne! nanka supootsu yatteta?
example.ja: 運動神経いいね！なんかスポーツやってた？
example.english: You're athletic! Did you use to play a sport?

examplePolite.romaji: undou shinkei ga ii desu ne! nanika supootsu yatteta n desu ka?
examplePolite.ja: 運動神経がいいですね！何かスポーツやってたんですか？
examplePolite.english: You're really athletic! Did you play a sport?

targets.trap: 'Fit' isn't fitto (in Japanese that's how clothes fit). genki covers 'well, healthy' (mada genki = still going strong), but for stamina and being in shape use tairyoku: tairyoku aru / tairyoku nai.
targets.use: Heard most in the negative, about age or being out of shape: mou tairyoku nai (I've got no stamina left), with ga dropped. Tairyoku aru ne praises someone who keeps going, and a drop in stamina is tairyoku ga ochita.
targets.notes: tairyoku o tsukeru (build up stamina) is the usual resolution: tairyoku tsukenakya.

example.romaji: saikin undou shitenai kara, tairyoku nai n da.
example.ja: 最近運動してないから、体力ないんだ。
example.english: I haven't been exercising lately, so I've got no stamina.

examplePolite.romaji: saikin undou shite inai node, tairyoku ga nai n desu.
examplePolite.ja: 最近運動していないので、体力がないんです。
examplePolite.english: I haven't been exercising lately, so I have no stamina.
